findings.title: Config key count and naming contradict the initiative plan and the architecture's own scope
findings.description: Description: The architecture introduces three global keys (`workflow.review_enabled`, `workflow.review_threshold`, `workflow.review_unknown_as`) plus a `workflow.review_gates` table. The initiative plan (`project-documents/user/project-guides/001-initiative-plan.context-forge.md:31`) specifies `workflow.review_required` and `workflow.review_threshold` — two keys. The input note (001-review-gating-architecture-input) says "240's two new keys are a direct addition here — no new config infrastructure needed" and lists exactly two. The architecture silently renames `review_required` → `review_enabled` and adds a third key plus a nested table, without flagging the divergence from the initiative plan that defines its scope. More importantly, the third key and the table are load-bearing: `review_unknown_as` changes the verdict semantics (UNKNOWN → CONCERNS → compared against threshold), and `review_gates` requires config infrastructure that does not exist. The architecture itself acknowledges this in Technical Considerations ("`ConfigKeyDefinition` interface supports scalar keys well but does not currently model nested tables") yet ships the nested table as a defined v1 artifact. Either align with the initiative plan's two-key scope, or explicitly record the deviation and its rationale.

findings.title: `ConfigKeyDefinition` cannot express the nested `review_gates` table, and the flat-namespace fallback breaks the config CLI and `ConfigManager.set`
findings.description: Description: `packages/core/src/config/ConfigKeys.ts:1-7` defines `ConfigKeyDefinition` with `type: 'string' | 'boolean' | 'number'` and a scalar `default`. `ConfigManager.get()` returns `value: string | boolean | number`; `ConfigManager.set()` takes `value: string | boolean | number` and calls `validateValue()`, which throws on a type mismatch against `def.type`. There is no object/table type. The architecture's proposed fallback — "treat `workflow.review_gates.*` as a flat namespace of dotted keys" — means keys like `workflow.review_gates.pre-advance.reviewType`, whose dotted path `resolveKey()` would traverse into the TOML table `[workflow.review_gates] pre-advance = { reviewType = "code" }` and resolve to `"code"`. That works for reading, but `cf config set workflow.review_gates.pre-advance.reviewType code` would call `setKey()`, which would create nested tables `{workflow: {review_gates: {pre-advance: {reviewType}}}}` — legal TOML, but `ConfigManager.set` requires the key to exist in `CONFIG_KEYS` or it throws "Unknown config key". So either way the per-gate overrides are unreachable through the existing config surface. The architecture defers the decision to "slice design time" while simultaneously listing the table in "Envisioned State" as a defined v1 artifact, and lists "per-gate override structure" as part of the first slice's deliverable. This decision must be made in the architecture, not deferred, because it determines whether slice 1 requires modifying `ConfigKeyDefinition`, `ConfigManager.get/set/list`, and the CLI `cf config set` contract.

findings.title: The `review` slot shape is unspecified and cannot represent the per-`reviewType` model the design requires
findings.description: Description: The architecture says "`DocumentDetectionResult` gains a `review` slot" and that the detector "scans `project-documents/user/reviews/` for files matching `NNN-review.{reviewType}.*.md` for the current slice index and configured reviewType." But `DocumentDetectionResult` (`packages/core/src/introspection/types.ts:68-73`) holds a single `string | null` per slot — `sliceDesign`, `architecture`, `slicePlan` — while `taskFile` is `string[] | null` because task files can be split. The config model here is explicitly multi-typed: one slice can have `arch`, `slice`, `tasks`, and `code` reviews, each matching a different `reviewType`, and the gate must look up one specific `reviewType` per transition. A single `review: string | null` cannot hold that. The architecture does not state the slot's type. If it is `string | null`, the detector must know the configured `reviewType` at detection time — but `detectDocuments(projectPath, sliceIndex)` has no config parameter and is called from `ArtifactIntrospector.detectDocuments()` (used by `ConsistencyChecker` and `ArtifactIntrospector.summarize()`), both of which are config-unaware. If it is a map or array, the "review slot" must be typed and the detection rule must return all review types, not filter by configured type. Either way this changes the `IArtifactIntrospector` interface — `packages/core/src/introspection/interfaces.ts:26` — which contradicts the architecture's claim in Related Work that "no 160 interfaces change."

findings.title: The `verdict`/`score` frontmatter contract is not enforced anywhere in CF, and the two docType schemas disagree
findings.description: Description: The architecture says CF "reads `verdict` and (when present) `score`" from the review artifact's frontmatter, and that the schema is owned by Squadron slice 300. But CF already owns a `review` docType schema in `packages/core/src/schema/frontmatterSchema.ts:97-104`, which requires only `docType`, `project`, `status`, `dateCreated`, `dateUpdated` — it does not include `verdict`, `score`, `criteria`, or `provenance`. Meanwhile `VALID_STATUSES` (`frontmatterSchema.ts:26-32`) is `not_started | in_progress | complete | deferred | deprecated` — `PASS`/`CONCERNS`/`FAIL`/`UNKNOWN` are not valid `status` values and would be flagged by Rule 12 (`ruleFrontmatterSchema`) as invalid only if placed in `status`. The architecture never states which frontmatter key carries the verdict (`verdict`? `status`?), nor that CF's `FRONTMATTER_SCHEMAS.review` must be extended to include `verdict`. This is a real cross-project contract collision that CF controls, and it is unresolved: if CF adds `verdict` to the review schema without `status` being one of the Squadron values, `cf check` will emit a frontmatter-schema error on every review document. That error would be indistinguishable from a genuine gate failure.

findings.title: `parseFrontmatter` cannot parse the `score`/`criteria`/`provenance` fields the design says CF reads and stores
findings.description: Description: The architecture states "Score-based gating (`score` field, float 0–100) is read and stored when present but not enforced in v1." The only frontmatter machinery in the introspection layer is `parseFrontmatter()` (`packages/core/src/introspection/parsers/frontmatterParser.ts`), which is a flat `key: value` string scanner: it splits on the first colon and stores the trimmed string. A `score: 87.5` would come back as the string `"87.5"`, and `criteria` as a YAML dict cannot be parsed at all — the parser would store the literal text after the first colon, e.g. `"{"a": 1, "b": 0.5}"`, on a single line. There is no YAML library in use here (the project uses `smol-toml` for TOML only). So "read and stored" is not achievable with the existing machinery without either a new YAML parse path or a hand-rolled numeric coercion. The architecture names no such work in its Anticipated Slices, and slice 1 is scoped to "the three global config keys and per-gate override structure" with no mention of frontmatter parsing changes. If the v1 requirement is only `verdict` (a plain scalar string), that should be stated and the score-reading claim dropped from v1 — it is exactly the kind of speculative extension the project's "resist adding complexity" principle forbids.

findings.title: `UNKNOWN` verdict handling is internally contradictory and produces an unreachable state
findings.description: Description: The "Slice status extension" section says `pending-review` means "tasks complete, review gate configured, no review artifact present (or verdict is `UNKNOWN` and `review_unknown_as` treats it as pending)". But `review_unknown_as` is declared with `default = "fail"` in the config block, and the Verdict handling section says UNKNOWN is "treated according to `workflow.review_unknown_as` (default: `fail`, therefore blocks)". So under defaults, UNKNOWN → `review-failed`, never `pending-review`. The `pending-review` parenthetical only applies under a non-default `review_unknown_as = "pending"`-style value — but the Technical Considerations section describes only two possible values for that key: `"fail"` and `"concern"`. There is no `"pending"` value defined anywhere, so the parenthetical describes a state that cannot be configured. Meanwhile a `CONCERNS` verdict under `review_unknown_as = "concern"` and `review_threshold = "concerns"` clears the gate, meaning a review artifact that literally says "I don't know" passes — the opposite of the stated "Conservative by default" goal. The verdict-to-status decision table needs to be a single explicit matrix with the actual legal values of `review_unknown_as`.

findings.title: The `pending-review` / `review-failed` gate only ever fires at one point, contradicting the four-transition config model
findings.description: Description: The config defines four transitions — `pre-slice-plan`, `pre-tasks`, `pre-implementation`, `pre-advance` — each with its own `reviewType` and `threshold`. But the gate is described as a single new priority branch inserted "between current Priority 5 (`in-implementation`) and Priority 6 (`complete → advance`)", and `deriveSliceStatus()` only sets the new statuses when `inferredStatus === 'complete'`. That branch can only ever consult the `pre-advance` gate. `pre-tasks` and `pre-implementation` have no insertion point: the `needs-tasks` and `in-implementation` branches fire before any review check, and the design never says a review for those transitions changes the slice status. So two of the four configured transitions are inert in v1 — yet `pre-tasks` and `pre-implementation` are presented in the Envisioned State as part of the defined config, and the Anticipated Slices list only four slices (discovery+config, gate logic, consistency rule, initiative-level gate) with no slice covering the `pre-tasks`/`pre-implementation` insertion points. Either scope v1 to `pre-advance` only, or specify where each transition's gate is evaluated.

findings.title: Worktree-scoped config resolution does not exist and the architecture asserts it as inherited capability
findings.description: Description: Related Work says "180-arch.initiative-context-worktree — Established worktree-scoped config resolution. The `workflow.review_*` keys should be resolvable at worktree scope (per-initiative review policy) as well as project scope, using the resolution chain 180 introduced." I verified the config layer: `packages/core/src/config/ConfigManager.ts` resolves exactly three scopes — project (`.context-forge.toml` at `projectPath`), user (`{storagePath}/config.toml`), then built-in default. There is no worktree scope in `configPaths.ts` or `ConfigManager`. The 180 architecture document describes worktree-scoped *workflow fields* (phase, slice, tasks, instructions) stored in the project's `worktrees[]` array — not config keys. Notably, `applyWorktreeOverlay` (`packages/core/src/utils/worktree-overlay.ts:9`) *does* replace `projectPath` with `wt.worktreePath`, so a project-scope `.context-forge.toml` in the worktree would be picked up incidentally — but that is a side effect of path substitution, not a "resolution chain 180 introduced", and it is not the per-initiative policy model the architecture describes. Additionally, `WorkflowNavigator` receives no `ConfigManager` at all today (`new WorkflowNavigator()` with no args in `packages/cli/src/commands/next.ts:26` and `packages/mcp-server/src/tools/workflowTools.ts:154`), so wiring config into the navigator is a constructor/dependency change that the architecture never mentions — it lists only `ConfigKeys.ts` and `documentDetector.ts` as files to change.

findings.title: The gate fires on a stale, unrelated review artifact because the lexicographic tiebreak is not a recency rule
findings.description: Description: "When multiple files match (e.g., two `code` review artifacts for the same index), the gate takes the lexicographically last filename (most recent by sort order). This is deterministic and documented." Lexicographic order on the filename suffix is not recency. The suffix is a free-form slug (e.g. `210-review.code.github-copilot-vs-code-ide-support.md`), so the "last" match is whichever slug sorts last alphabetically — `zebra-review` beats `zulu-final-review` regardless of which was written later. The parenthetical "(most recent by sort order)" asserts an equivalence that does not hold. There is no mtime in the selection rule, and no rule at all for which artifact wins when a later review supersedes an earlier one. This matters because re-running a review produces a second artifact with a different slug (e.g. `...-rerun.md`), and the gate would silently evaluate whichever slug sorts last, not whichever was written last. The rule as written is also surprising in the opposite direction: it makes the gate outcome depend on slug naming, not on artifact content or write order.

findings.title: `review-failed` maps to a `blocked` recommendation with no consumer-visible contract, and `NextAction.recommendation` is free-form
findings.description: Description: The architecture promises Amoeba's Runner that "the gate must not change the `NextAction` return type, only add new `recommendation` string values." But `NextAction.recommendation` is typed `string` (`packages/core/src/introspection/types.ts:281`) and every existing value is a human-readable sentence, not a token: `"Set projectPath"`, `"Create architecture document"`, `` `Advance to slice ${nextEntry.index}: ${nextEntry.name}` ``, `` `Continue implementation — ${remaining} task${remaining !== 1 ? 's' : ''} remaining` ``. The new values `"review"` and `"blocked"` are the first bare tokens in a free-form string field. A downstream runner that dispatches on `recommendation` cannot distinguish them by type or by pattern — it must string-compare against two magic literals that are not declared anywhere as a contract (no exported constant, no enum, no union type). The document's own Design Goal says runners "can act on them without parsing recommendation strings" — but the mechanism for doing that (a typed recommendation vocabulary) is exactly what is missing. Related: "Conservative by default... `review_enabled = false`" also implies the runner must distinguish a gated `review` from an ungated recommendation, which again requires a stable vocabulary.

findings.title: The `review_unknown_as = "concern"` semantics are documented as a support hazard but not designed around
findings.description: Description: "When `review_unknown_as = "concern"`, `UNKNOWN` is treated as `CONCERNS` and then compared against `review_threshold`. This means the same `UNKNOWN` artifact can pass or block depending on the threshold — which is the intended behavior but must be documented clearly to avoid support confusion." The mitigation offered is documentation. Given the project's explicit rule — "Never use silent fallback values. Fail explicitly with errors or obviously-placeholder values" — mapping `UNKNOWN` to `CONCERNS` (a passing verdict) is precisely a silent fallback that launders an unknown outcome into a pass. The safer and simpler design is `review_unknown_as` accepting only `fail` (block) and `error` (surface as a distinct error), or dropping the key entirely and always blocking on UNKNOWN, which is already the default. The two-value model as designed has a state (`UNKNOWN` + `concern`) where a review that cannot be parsed — including the malformed-YAML case the Technical Considerations section explicitly wants to surface — results in a *passing* gate. The design contradicts its own "Conservative by default" goal and its own "File-read failure modes... must not silently pass" requirement.

findings.title: The consistency-checker rule duplicates gate logic that the architecture says must live in one place
findings.description: Description: The new `ConsistencyChecker` rule re-derives "artifact absent" and "verdict does not clear the threshold" from the same inputs as the gate — the same verdict vocabulary, the same threshold comparison, the same `review_unknown_as` policy, the same per-transition `reviewType` mapping. The architecture states "the gate lives in the shared `WorkflowNavigator` and `ConsistencyChecker`" as a single inheritance mechanism, but `ConsistencyChecker` and `WorkflowNavigator` are separate classes with no shared gate component; neither takes a `ConfigManager`; and `ConsistencyChecker` runs a *different* slice set than the navigator (all-slices mode via `checkAll()`, which iterates plan entries). The verdict-comparison logic will exist in two places unless a shared, config-aware gate module is extracted. Per the project's CLAUDE.md ("Do not duplicate logic. Respect DRY"), the architecture should specify a single `ReviewGate` component that both call — and it must be config-aware, which no current component is.

findings.title: The `pre-slice-plan` transition is defined in v1 config but its gate is deferred, which produces a config key that silently does nothing
findings.description: Description: The config block ships `pre-slice-plan = { reviewType = "arch", threshold = "pass" }` as an example users will copy into `.context-forge.toml`, but the gate logic is a later slice and v1 "implements only the four slice-level transitions" — a sentence that is itself contradictory, since `pre-slice-plan` is an initiative-level transition and the four named transitions are `pre-slice-plan`/`pre-tasks`/`pre-implementation`/`pre-advance`, of which only one (`pre-advance`) is actually implemented in v1 per the gate-insertion-point section. A user who configures `pre-slice-plan` gets no gating and no diagnostic. The document's own "Fail-fast on configuration errors" principle argues for rejecting unknown/unimplemented transition keys at config validation time rather than accepting them silently.

findings.title: The `review` slot added to `DocumentDetectionResult` affects a shared MCP output surface
findings.description: Description: `DocumentDetectionResult` is returned directly by the MCP `introspection_documents` tool (`packages/core/src/introspection/interfaces.ts:26`, exercised by `packages/mcp-server/tests/introspectionTools.test.ts:256`). Adding a `review` slot changes that tool's response shape. The architecture scopes itself to "Config keys, a review-artifact discovery mechanism in the document detector, new slice status values, the gate logic in `WorkflowNavigator`, and a new consistency rule" and states "no 160 interfaces change" — but the MCP tool's output shape does change. This is additive and probably acceptable, but it belongs in the document as a noted surface change rather than claimed as zero interface change.

findings.title: Renumbering the priority cascade is bundled into the discovery/config slice as incidental work
findings.description: Description: "Includes renumbering the `getNext()` priority cascade" is placed in the *first* slice, which is otherwise "No gate logic yet — this is the foundation the gate builds on." But `getNext()`'s branch comments are the only record of the cascade's ordering, and the current numbering is already non-contiguous (`Priority 2.5` sits between 2 and 3 at `WorkflowNavigator.ts:187`). Renumbering the whole cascade in a slice that adds no behavior creates a large, conflict-prone diff against a file that slice 2 will then modify again. Converting to named stages (as the architecture itself suggests as an alternative) would be the cleaner move, but it should be its own slice, not folded into the discovery/config slice.
